utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have French on channel four. Good morning, Mr. Barkovic. I would like to remind that you you're still by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, we left off at the end of yesterday discussing the reassignment of Major Werner Ilic. And just to recap, the major was assigned to take the MPRI courses which were designed to teach him how to teach other NCOs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you gave us some explanations yesterday about why the major was dissatisfied with his assignment. One of the reasons indicated in General Griffiths' letter that we read yesterday was that Major Ilic didn't see the value of the programme itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was Major Ilic eventually permitted to return to his unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you aware of whether or not Major Ilic was disciplined for having failed to report to the MPRI classes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, what message do you think it sends not only to Major Ilic but to the other HV soldiers he may have discussed the MPRI classes, what message do you think it sent to them about the MPRI classes and how valuable they were, given that Major Ilic was simply permitted not to show up?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was definitely not a good message. But it's clear that if someone does not want to be an instructor, he or she cannot be forced to do so. And Major Ilic did not join from the very start. He came later. So I don't know if this is an alleviating circumstance. He was not familiar with the whole programme in the first place. He was just included in the first stage of preparatory courses, so he was never able to have insight into the whole of those programmes. And later, he attended the Main Staff school and we had never any problems of intolerance with him, so I don't think he spread any disinformation or fueled any problems with the democracy assistance transition programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. But you would agree with me and with the sentiments expressed by Major-General Cosic, that Major Ilic's unilateral decision to simply stop going to the class was not appropriate and, in fact, warranted discipline?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may, that is not what the Cosic letter says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies. That's correct. Only the first portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's my assertion that that warranted discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we split that up. I mean, if we go back to the Cosic letter and read the Cosic letter and ask the question there, it may be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, will you please rephrase your question in such a way that it accurately reflects what you're referring to, and perhaps take one step by one step.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You would agree with Major-General Cosic that Major Ilic's unilateral decision to stop going to the classes was inappropriate conduct, unbecoming of a HV officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that when an officer, or when a NCO, or a soldier or anyone in the HV army takes such inappropriate unilateral action that it warrants discipline?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President at this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 7276. That's the Cosic and Griffiths letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Russo, would you allow me one additional question. Mr. Barkovic, could you explain your answer that, as you said, it is clear that someone who does not want to be an instructor, he or she cannot be forced to do so. Isn't it true that in a military structure that you have to obey what orders you get and that, if you don't obey them, that you can be forced, or at least measures can be taken such that either do you it or negative consequences will follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I mean, these two things are not mutually contrary. I know as a teacher that a person who does not really wish to teach others but is forced to do so is not going to do a good job any way. So if somebody does not want to be a teacher or instructor, it is better to remove them. On the other hand, I agree with you that the person who does not obey orders in the army should be sanctioned. However, here again, we have to bear in mind the environment in which all this was happening. We had put together teams of American officers and Croatian officers in November 1994, and within a month, we sized up the situation, made a baseline assessment, put it in a document; and then, in January, we prepared an instructor training programme for NCOs, because we had noticed certain shortcomings before, and at the beginning of that course, Werner Ilic appeared at the MPRI. Did he not really know where he was going and what he would be doing there, and his personal qualities made him blow his stack, in a way. He had come from America to Croatia to defend the country, and when his disciplinary liability was evaluated, I think this circumstance was also taken into account, and, as a result, he was only reprimanded and told that this kind of conduct was not acceptable, and he was given another job that he was able and willing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Line 5 or page 5. I lost it. Line 6 the circumstances under which Mr. Werner Ilic appeared were not -- did not get translated. He didn't just appear there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of preparations, we had received a very short order consisting of only two items, saying that Werner Ilic, Major Werner Ilic was to join, and, on the next day he arrived pursuant to that order. We found him accommodate addition at the barracks, and on the third day after this order he started to work. That's what I meant by saying he appeared. Did he not appear of his own free will. He been sent pursuant to an order, sent and signed, I believe, by General Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions. I do appreciate your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President I have a few matters to cover with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to Major Ilic, Major Ilic came -- was it your testimony that Major Ilic came to be an instructor, to will learn how to be an instructor at this MPRI school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, all of our instructors did two jobs. On the one hand, based on their abilities they already had, they prepared other people to become instructors the best they could, and some who came for the first time to prepare themselves to become instructors attended this instructor training course. Major Ilic was to join the group of people who already were instructors and who were following an advanced programme to become better instructor, and, at the same time, to prepare new men to become instructors and there were many of those, many NCOs that needed advanced training. So formally speaking, Major Ilic was sent to us as an instructor, although he did not have the necessary abilities and training for that. He had relatively little experience in training -- in the training of soldiers and NCOs but mainly in practical skills, and not in any academic skills that would enable him to educate others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe there is an issue with the transcript that Mr. Misetic will cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could ask for -- at page 6, line 24 the witness described the purpose for which Mr. Ilic was sent to this MPRI programme which didn't get picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've heard the question. Could you please clarify the purpose for which Mr. Ilic was sent to this programme.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Ilic was sent to become part of the instructor team that was to prepare, both instructor training courses, and after that, regular courses. However, all our instructors prepared at the same time to be better instructors and ran courses themselves. That is difficult to understand perhaps but because we had limited time, that's the way we had to do it. We prepared very intensively training and then we carried out that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, in P2558 [sic], the document from General Cosic and the attached letter from General Griffiths, it notes in paragraph 5 that Major Ilic requested relief from his assignment. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. But he didn't ask that of me or of General Griffiths, the people who led the programme. He instead sent a letter to the Chief of the Main Staff and the minister of defence saying that he was unwilling to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall General Griffiths, in paragraph 5, noting that, "In my view, Major Ilic is unsuited for assignment," and going down two sentences, "Major Ilic is a young, immature, unstable ... and overly impressed with himself." Do you recall that being as -- the consensus or the view of Major Griffiths concerning Major Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed that, so, in fact, it was our joint opinion. We all agreed that Major Ilic had strayed into that programme which required more systematic and quiet work than he was suited for, with his energy and level of preparedness. So that might be the reason why he acted the way he acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Apologies I just want to point out, page 7, line 18, the exhibit should read P2588.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I don't know if I misspoke there, counsel, but thank you for the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this discuss you had with Major Ilic, you then had a discussion with General Cosic prior to this letter that was sent to the minister of defence, Minister Susak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if we had a discussion or not, but we did write down what we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did everybody -- all of the -- the people that were part of the decision-making agree that Major Ilic was unsuitable for this task and that he should be sent back to his original unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given that this was the result, I believe that General Cosic did as he wrote here, i.e., that he consulted the personnel service, General Gotovina and brigadier, as he was at the time, Sundov, who was I think in the 4th Brigade, and they agreed what to do, how, where to send Major Ilic for his assignment, taking into account our proposal and the fact that he was not a suitable person for our job in the programme. He was not happy with us and we didn’t think –- we thought we were better off without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sounds like my first marriage. Just kidding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the second any better, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second was much better, Mr. President, I must say, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to change topics and just cover some of the things by Mr. Russo discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And turning first to P2559, and I believe this is discussed, Mr. President, beginning on page 20197 going on to 20198, if we could bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could go first to the last page of this document, which is -- maybe the second to last page, paragraph 210 which was the focus of Mr. Russo's inquiries, and we will then come back to the first page, but I would just like to touch on the last page first. In the topic that we were discussing yesterday -- you were discussed yesterday with Mr. Russo is 2.10 turning to proposals for commendations for officers, non-commissioned officers, and lower ranks by segments included in the attack operation will be submitted later. Now, you were asked some questions about these proposals and recommendations, but I -- and you noted there were no names listed, but I would like to go back to this chain of this document and if we could back to the first page. Now, Professor, in the chain you noticed that there is a -- this is being executed by General Gotovina pursuant to your order class, and you see the reference number there as well as the -- the class number and the reference number of August 8th. Would it be fair to say that this is a response to an order to him? And let us go to 65 ter 5634.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the document on the screen is 65 ter 5634, and I will tell you that -- Professor, that the class and serial number that are in this document midway through on the left-hand side match that in General Gotovina's order. And as we noted from P2559, it's dated the 15th of August, and this is an order coming from General Cervenko, dated 8 August where he notes in 1: "Data should be gathered, also the operation carried out should be analysed, and by 15 August 1995, you should submit to me in written form detailed reports, conclusions, and proposals concerning the following issues." And if we could turn to the next page in the English and the next page in the B/C/S in the section for B it starts with conclusions and proposals for promotion. And under that paragraph, if we go down to the last bullet, we go conclusions and proposals for promotion, and it notes for the commendation of officer, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers according to segments and reads on. So based on your experience in the HV would you conclude looking at these two documents that General Gotovina was responding to this order from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is highly leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would ask him -- I withdraw the question. I'll just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on these two documents and based on your experience, sir, putting these two documents together, the order from the Main Staff and General Gotovina's order, tell the Chamber what your conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing the function of a military operation and the principle of unified command, I think that these two documents clearly show that on the 8th of August, the Chief of Main Staff ordered an analysis to be done, and in that analysis, he required which items should be included and he also ordered to draw conclusions and draft recommendations for the purpose of the enhancement of a number of issues, which is the -- which concerned the way of the -- how a military organisation functions. We also saw that this is classified as highly urgent, this order. And from the first document in which General Gotovina replied to that, we see that a week later, that within that week, the analysis was conducted and put on paper, and in that analysis, the answers to these questions were given. So we can conclude that he acted in accordance with -- with the order of the Chief of General Staff. If we were to refer to item 2.10, we could say that he was careful enough. He wasn't hasty, and he said that the proposals for commendations would be submitted subsequently. So he gave himself enough time to consider with his subordinate officers who was -- who acted well enough during the Storm operation so as to be eligible for a commendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe Mr. Misetic had another note -- okay, I thought there was another mistake in the transcript, and I trust that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, Professor, if President Tudjman gave an order to give medals to people who participated in Storm and Flash, independent of commendations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you something and see if it refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to show this via Sanction, and this would be 1D2783.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I ask to you take a look at this document, Professor, being a decision from the president and does that refresh your recollection as to this -- the sequence of events by President Tudjman? And, by the way, this is dated 7 August 1995, concerning giving medals for Flash, Operation Storm, and for others that participated in the liberation in Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, and Banja, as well as Summer 95, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I know what you meant. It is usual not only in the Croatian army but in all armies of the world to -- to introduce medals for the participation in certain military operations, so that for Storm and other operations, such medals were introduced, and they were given to all who took part in them. As far as I know, those medals were not an acknowledgment for special undertakings but rather all soldiers, NCOs, and officers received that medal merely for their participation in those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, I'd will offer into evidence 1D2783, and likewise as I'm doing with the prior document which is 65 ter 5634, which is the 8th of August order by General Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection to either document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Start with the 8th of August order, 65 ter 5634, which was introduced by --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit D1605 and the second document, 1D2783, will become Exhibit D1606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both documents are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Barkovic, based on your experience in the HV, would an order such as that then be filtered down to -- through the Main Staff to individual commanders to give a list of people who were eligible for such a -- a medal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And due to the relatively large span of command from the level right below the Chief of General Staff down to the level of platoons, certain time was necessary to do all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you P1184 that's in evidence, which is an order from General Gotovina dated 16 August 1995 to all units of the Split Military District. If you take a look at this document. In the preamble, it notes: "Pursuant to item 23 of the rules, rules of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia ... in accordance with the order of the chief of the personnel administration of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia ... of 14 August 1995, and in order to create optimal [sic] conditions to carry out the decision of the president of the Republic of Croatia establishing a medal for participating in military police [sic] operations, I hereby issue the following for successful completion of military and police operations Summer 95 and Storm, based on this order" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe you read optimal where the text on my screen reads "operational."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, operational. My apologies. If we can scroll down this on page 1: "... for successful completion of the military and police operations, Summer 95 and Storm, based on this order, all members of the units of the Croatian army who took part in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District are eligible to receive ..." and it has a medal for Storm in 1.2 and a medal for Summer 95. Now, again, do you see any link between these documents and, if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the last three documents, from the order given by the Chief of General Staff, then the order given by General Gotovina, and this order right here that we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about Tudjman -- the President Tudjman directive and this order by General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] The decision of President Tudjman was to introduce medals for certain military operations. General Gotovina's order for the period of defining the shape, et cetera, of these medals, was to find out who took part in the operation. I can see an item here mentioning all those who, for any reason, were not present in a combat zone as excluded from this; and as we see, the medals for participation should be given to the members of all units in operations Summer 95 and Storm which actually followed one another, all those -- all those who took part there were to receive medals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me -- by the way, just to clarify the document itself, you were referring to, I believe, paragraph 3 and 4 -- paragraph 3: "All members of units are eligible to receive medal for their participation in the operations from this order regardless of the time spent in the unit during the operations." And paragraph 4: "Members who are absent from their unit for the duration of the operations because of illness or other reasons shall not be eligible." Just for clarity on the record, sir, are those the two paragraphs that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to shift topics just for a moment and cover some of the discussion that you had yesterday with Mr. Russo concerning work by the NCOs and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you would allow me, I would like to seek some clarification of a matter which is not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Barkovic, what we have seen is an order by President Tudjman of the 7th of August, which more or less introduces a kind of -- could I say automatic rewarding all those who participated with a medal; and we see that on this document of the 14th further data are sought to be collected in order to find out who they are. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe that's the 16th, Mr. President. The order by General Gotovina is the 16th, P1184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. Yes, that's the 16th, I apologise for this lack of precision. Now, apart from that, we have the order by General Cervenko of the 8th, in which he asks for an analysis; and the response dated the 15th of August by General Gotovina in which he says, Well, commendations for -- and I think it covered both medals but also, for example, promotions. You received that at a later stage. Now, what I'd like to know is whether this is the same exercise. Did the automatic granting medals for those who participated, did that replace the commendation for specific officers, non-commissioned officers, soldiers to receive promotion or to receive medals of whatever kind? Are these -- is it the same, or are these two different exercises, the one being the automatic issuing medals to all participants; and the second, which appears to me, from what I've seen until now, to be a more individualised exercise so as to find out who, not just for their participation, but on the basis of their behaviour, would -- would deserve to be issued a medal or to be promoted? Is it the same exercise or are these two different exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these are definitely two separate exercises. The one that -- one that starts with the decision to introduce a medal and continues with the finding out who really participated, and the other exercise was to give commendations, et cetera, to those who -- who had outstanding achievements. That is, who stood out from everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to shift gears if we can, Professor, and go back to the issue of NCOs, and I would like to take you back in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we are talking, Mr. President, about page 20204, and the question by Mr. Russo that -- concerning NCOs and achievements of objectives: "Q. He says doesn't this show, Professor, that it is not a problem of lack of training or a problem of insufficient NCOs when the NCOs have a job to do that they're interested in doing, they get it done. Wasn't that the case? Your answer in line 7: "In one of my answer, I explained that the NCOs have three types of tasks. Some of which they can achieve better and others poorer. It is down to their technical and tactical levels of training, the spirit, morale, and discipline of the unit. These objectives could have been achieved if the level of training and tactical activity was good, even if the morale or discipline was not. These are two separate issues." Now, let me, once again, address for you D204, which is General Gotovina's order that we discussed very briefly yesterday of 10 August 1995. And you can read the preamble, but the subject is order on compliance with military discipline and measures. And number 1 is: "I prohibit arbitrary movement of HV members in the liberated areas, without the knowledge of their superior commanders." Now I will tell you, sir, that during the course of the evidence received by this Chamber from a member of a Home Guard Regiment, a question was asked by a member of the Chamber, and I'm referring to page 19644, question beginning at line 15 to 20 by Judge Kinis, where a question was posed to this member of the Home Guards who did some control over you, over behaviour of soldiers at that time. You said you didn't know who your superior -- you didn't know who is your platoon commander, and so -- but who -- was there actually some kind of control over behaviour of soldiers where soldiers were freely to move during -- during the night wherever they want? "A. No." Now, sir, can you explain that type of issue where a witness would say there is no control over their behaviour and General Gotovina has to issue an order on the 10th of August to prohibit arbitrary movement of HV members?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to object. This is re-direct examination, and the witness is being fed information and led to particular conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- I am taking the questions that were asked by Mr. Russo, where he noted, again on pages 20203 and 4, where he posited the premises that simply because military measures during Operation Storm were completed, that indicated that there was, in fact, no problem at the NCO level. And that's the point I'm attempting to address, and it also goes back, once again, to the question that Judge Kinis asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. At the same time, I add to this, that when these questions were put by Mr. Russo yesterday, if the result is good, doesn't that mean that the NCOs were functioning well, that on the basis of the apparent lack of firsthand information by this witness, because we are looking at documents whether the -- whether the operation was successful or not, that the most could be said on the basis of those documents, that, at least, a lack of training was not an obstacle to the success. That's the most you could say about it, trying to -- without further detailed analysis, to see what exactly the causes of the success were -- was an exercise which made no sense. I add this, that also might limit your interest in trying to do similar things to -- to try to draw all kind of conclusions from documents. Again, I'm not talking about someone who has firsthand knowledge, but to draw all kind of conclusions on the basis of documents which allow for many conclusions, for those who have not observed and have not analysed the exact causes of what happened. Mr. Kehoe, I had this on my mind yesterday, but I didn't intervene when Mr. Russo was examining the witness on the subject, but if this will have a follow-up with a similar relatively meaningless exercise, I would -- I would like to inform you that that came to my mind yesterday and similar things might come to my mind if you continue on this subject. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I believe you, Mr. President, when you said with this particular question the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He can answer the question, but, again, if we draw conclusions which are as debatable as the conclusions that Mr. Russo tried to elicit yesterday, then we do not move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. We can change subjects, Mr. President and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave it to you. As I said before, the witness may answer the question, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just have the witness answer the question briefly, and we will change subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Professor ...

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can repeat that various tasks can be carried out at various levels of quality, and I think that issues of discipline are something specific. It has to do with combat activity but especially with what's happening with the army when they are not fighting. After the victory, there is some sort of relaxation, probably different kinds of partying going on, and -- well, the behaviour is then -- they behave according. The behaviour of NCOs is very important in that context, and we see here that disciplinary measures are very important to prevent the soldiers from doing what they're not supposed to do. Among them, the limitation of movement. That contributes not only to the safety and the combat readiness of soldiers but also -- it can also affect things that soldiers might do if they were to move arbitrarily in the circumstances as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, let us shift to our final topic on this area, and it goes to the issues of discipline in concerning Grahovo and Glamoc that Mr. Russo discussed with you yesterday and matters that were brought to your attention in the diary of the Split Military District, P71. And the first issue that I would like to talk to you about is -- and in some decision is on page 20187, 20187, my apologies. And the question was asked: "Q. Well, in particular, he," turning to General Gotovina, "was aware of the fact that the soldiers that he was going to use for Operation Storm were inclined to loot and burn Serb property; isn't that right?" Your answer: "I can't say what he thought about that. He probably had reason to suspect there might be undisciplined behaviour, but his mission was so serious and so great that he had to reckon with certain risks in that area." Now, your discussion about this mission being so great and so serious that he had to reckon with certain risks in that area, tell us what you're talking about there.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that he couldn't engage larger forces, or because he probably didn't have enough forces, to maintain security in an area where the first major operations were already completed. So he had to use the forces to secure the flanks because these things can jeopardise the units, and in that situation, much more can happen than can usually be expected from soldiers and their behaviour, and this is what we said, that a -- in the rear, that some people would behave inadequately and obviously he tried to react to that in such orders in which he -- he pointed out to the lower level commanders what risks they were. So he could have minimised these risks, but that would have jeopardised the achievement of the greater goals. This merely has to do with the resources that were at his disposal for these two different kinds of tasks, military resources, I mean, the strength of the forces, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, if I may, to a question that was asked by Mr. Russo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could we first try to establish the factual basis on which the last answer is based. First of all, you started your answer put to you by Mr. Russo by saying: "I can't say what he thought about that. He probably had reason to suspect that there might be undisciplined behaviour, but his mission was so great," et cetera. Now in your answer to Mr. Kehoe's question, you introduced, you said: "And obviously he tried to react to that in such orders in which he, he pointed out to the lower level commanders what risks there were." Could you give us an example of such an order in which he pointed out to the lower level commanders what risks there were, because that's a new element in your answer. Could you tell us about one of these orders? At what moment did he point at these risks, orders to the lower commanders? Could you give us an example of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't. This whole story is not based on my direct knowledge but on the documents I've seen here, and I believe this order we are looking at now shows such initiatives. This one is postdated, but I think it's logical that this train of thought yields suggestions of the kind that we see after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware -- have you any reason to believe that such orders in which risks were pointed out -- that lower commanders were given at the start or prior to the start of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have, based on my general experience, general combat experience, the way soldiers think. Nothing more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, let's try to refrain from assumptions, expectations, and, rather, focus on known facts to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was taking that as a lead-in to these final documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, you were shown documents by -- in the war diary of the Split Military District by Mr. Russo from the latter part of July of 1991 -- excuse me, 1995. And in page 20186, where Mr. Russo is talking about particular orders, he notes on page 13 [sic]: "Q. And you agree with me, wouldn't you, that when an order such as that is issued and it is not effective and it is not followed, that it doesn't behoove the commander to simply reissue the same order and hope it gets obeyed the second time?" Your answer: "No. Measures of control and inspection must be taken. Personal control at one's own level and two levels below, see what's happening, why it's happening, learn the lessons and get to the bottom of that and then achieve appropriate conduct." On page 20193 you were -- at line, 6 Mr. Russo asked the question: "Would you also agree with me, wouldn't you, that if measures weren't taken after Grahovo and Glamoc to address the looting and burning that had created a further risk of the same conduct continuing in the aftermath of Operation Storm; isn't that right?" Your answer is: "Yes. Now, let's take the first part of that issue first. You note that in line 19 on 20186, that when improper conduct comes to the attention of a commander, he must get to the bottom of it. And I want to turn your attention to a part of the diary that was not shown to you yesterday by Mr. Russo, and that would be P71, page 69 in the English and page 34 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep seeing the same documents on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We are bringing up another document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah. Just to take you back, Professor Barkovic, Mr. Russo showed you some excerpts of this yesterday. I've just shown you another excerpt for 1 August 1995, three days prior to Operation Storm. And if you read with me about midway down ... And this is a comment by General Gotovina, as you see on the left-hand column -- I'm sorry, I'm being informed this is not the right page. If we can go to the next column, please, in the B/C/S. Is that right? There it is. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a comment by General Gotovina. He notes that the biggest problem in OG Sjever, Sjever is north, OG North, you can see that translation a couple of lines above. The biggest problem in OG Sjever --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- is the lack of discipline, so we ordered to the commanders of the units to pay attention and strictly forbid looting and burning. Now if the commander of OG North, sir, based on your answers to Mr. Russo, is not sufficiently enforcing discipline to prevent looting and burning, is there a remedy that General Gotovina can re-employ with regard to the commander of OG North?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going object to the question. The portion which was read doesn't indicated an order to the commander of OG North. It indicates orders to the commanders of the units to pay attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This -- this says, The biggest problem is the lack of discipline, so we order to the commanders of the units to pay attention and strictly forbid looting and burning. This is units that are part of OG North, and the OG North commander commands those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's try to -- to avoid all kind of exegetic exercises. What Mr. Kehoe apparently wants to know, Mr. Barkovic, is what General Gotovina should have done, if there was such a lack of discipline, what would have been the remedy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the commander of OG North.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, or -- I take it that since orders were issued to the commanders as well, why not include commander of Sector North or any of his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's -- OG North, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: OG -- yes, I'm sorry. What -- what would have been the appropriate remedy if, apparently, the discipline was not such as General Gotovina wished it to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is also one of the ways in which, at the meeting of all commanders at briefings, one specific group and one specific commander are warned that the situation in their unit is not good. To a good soldier, that is quite enough, to motivate him to take appropriate steps, disciplined building steps. Of course, if there was not enough time, as there was not enough time on the 1st of August, perhaps a meeting one-on-one with the commander, or with a specific unit would be a good beginning in building up discipline in a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say "not enough time on the 1st of August," were you aware that Operation Storm began at approximately 5.00 in the morning on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is an appropriate remedy to curtail improper conduct by people under the command of OG North the removal of that commander? Is a possible remedy to attempt to curtail improper conduct by troops under the command of operation north [sic] the removal of the commander of operation north?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you asking for a possible remedy or the appropriate remedy because when you repeated your question, you choose different wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm saying a possible remedy at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this point. So you should focus your answer on whether that was a possible remedy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That might have been a possible solution, but it would involve great risks, because that same commander had undergone long preparations for executing the operation. He had the concept of the entire operation. He knew the mission of his particular unit better than any other member of the commanding corps. He, based on all that, issued instructions and orders that were studied by the unit. If you change the commander a few days before the operation, that would perhaps address some disciplinary problems but would cause many more great problems in the whole functioning of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, Professor Barkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, this is an order of 3 August 1995 by General Gotovina: "In keeping with the order for the attack of the commander of the Split Military District ... and with the purpose of having a uniform command and control of the units: Order. Staff Brigadier Rahim Ademi is temporarily appointed commander of OG North. He shall perform the said duty alongside his established [sic] duty. "The outgoing commander of the OG North, Colonel Slaven Zdilar," pardon my pronunciation, "is to resume his duty as acting chief of infantry of the Split Military District. "This order shall come into effect immediately." Going back, Professor Barkovic, to the question asked by Mr. Russo, do you consider this order at this time, at this juncture, a measure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- should we first ask the witness whether he knows what the reasons were that Staff Brigadier Ademi is temporarily appointed. Let's first ask what he knows about it. Do you know what caused this replacement of the commander of the Operation Group North? Do you know the background? Do you know why it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, where the witness doesn't know, of course, we can start imagining whether this would have been the reason. Apparently the witness doesn't know the reasons why, and I'd like you to accept that as a lack of factual knowledge in this respect by this witness when you proceed with your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect when Mr. Russo asked the hypothetical question, there was no stopping of that question. If you turn to page 20193, the page -- line 6 to line 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo was cross-examining the witness, and where leading questions, that is, questions which are either suggesting an answer or in which facts are suggested which have not yet been established, is permissible; whereas, that's not the case in-chief. Apart from that, of course, the Chamber would like to have testimony which assists it, and, therefore, it's of great importance -- I'm not saying that you can't ask any questions about this order. I just wanted to establish what the witness does know and doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as I said earlier in respect of a certain matter yesterday, that it was more or less seeking -- well, if you say, Let me go ahead because you didn't stop Mr. Russo, please go ahead but please be also aware that this, of course, is important information for the Chamber to evaluate the evidence the witness will give on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand the guidance, and if we go through the sequence of the information that Mr. Russo presented to the witness concerning burning and looting and asking that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my problem is that this witness testifies that he has got no idea why this was happening. It might be that the mother of the gentleman fell ill or -- we do not know, and we have to keep that in mind, and I let you proceed. Please keep this in mind that the factual knowledge of the witness is extremely limited, as he just told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First, Professor Barkovic, this particular change in command less than 24 hours prior to Storm, or approximately 24 hours, based on your military experience is that a radical move by professor -- by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly is a radical move. And thinking of what we had discussed before, if these two things are linked, I would really be impressed. If that was linked to the meeting held two days prior. A mitigating circumstance that you see, it is well thought out, because General Gotovina put in the position of commander a man who had great combat experience and had cooperated with him before, and if he -- the Staff Brigadier Ademi was aware of all that the commander had studied before in preparation, et cetera, then that would have meant an optimal solution to the problem, replacing the commander just before the operation by a man who really knows all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, would -- based on your military experience, would such a decision on the change of the command at the operative group level, would that reverberate down to the troops in the field?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It certainly would. But adversely, or positively, I wouldn't be able to say, because I did not know what kind of feelings the subordinates had harboured towards the previous commander who was replaced and what they thought of the new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. I appreciate your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Cermak Defence or Markac Defence, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Nothing arising, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No question, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Barkovic, I have one specific question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about -- and let me try to find it. If you give me one second, I will try to find the exact wording. You told us that you had put together teams of American officers and Croatian officers in November 1994. Could you give us more details about what they did, what was the basis for putting those teams together?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, the minister of defence had signed a contract with a private company, MPRI, an American company, about carrying out a democratic transition assistance programme in the armed forces. That programme was based on a technical proposal similar to the one we have in evidence. We don't have that original document, but I don't think it's so relevant for this process. That programme was geared towards lending assistance in management and personal management in the armed forces under the circumstances of embargo. So all elements related to any combat training were excluded from the programme. That was one limitation. In the month of November, we formed a team to evaluate the situation, consisting of five American officers and five Croatian officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there to seek further clarification. Were these active US army officers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, retired officers. All of them were retired officers and one of them was a NCO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they were not, to say so, on the payroll of the US army at that moment anymore. Were they all employed by the company which provided this assistance? Because there might be some confusion if we're talking about cooperation between American officers, whether they were active-duty officers or not, they were not. So the teams consisted of former army officers, and you said one non-commissioned officer, which were employed by a private company. Was there any -- was there any involvement of the United States government in hiring the MPRI, in financing the programme? Could you tell us whether there was any such link or whether there was not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme was approved by the US government, but the government did not participate in the funding. The funding was provided by the Croatian state, and the project and the contents of the project had been approved by the US government, because an embargo was in place at the time, and they had to decide whether the contents of the programme were consistent with the embargo. That's why we could not include combat training in the programme. May I now continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, this was the primary purpose of my question, to find out exactly -- because I was a bit confused by the term "officers" where it was unclear it me whether they were active officers or whether they were retired officers. If you want to add one or two lines, that's fine with me. But the question that I wanted to put in not too much a leading way has been answered. So I leave it to you whether you want to add one or two lines.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly. Every pair of officers, one American, one Croatian active-duty officer, made an evaluation for one level of training, NCO officer, commander, and staff level, and the functioning of the staff, those five elements were evaluated. We made this evaluation in end 1994, and in 1995, after adopting the baseline assessment, we went forward with advanced training for NCOs, officer, commanding officers, and staff officers, providing personnel management training, which is a linkage between what we do in the education system and how these people will be ran in the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions of you. Has the question of the Bench triggered any need for further questions or is there -- Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Barkovic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for the answers you've given when

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first have a break. The next witness is available. The parties will have received last Friday, because it was a matter which seemed to be urgent to the extent that for preparation of the testimony of the next witness, that at least the parties would have some guidance as where the thoughts of the Chamber, in which direction the thoughts of the Chamber provisionally went. I take it that message is received, and that whether that leads to any adaptation of your way of questioning the witness, that is to what extent, 92 ter and to what extent viva voce, I do not know. But are there any questions about this or is it clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the remark you just made triggered a question on my part. The basis for the objection that we made was that the portions of the statement were expert opinion and hadn't been tendered through the proper procedure, and I understood the e-mail from the Chamber to indicate that those paragraphs -- that the Chamber was hesitant to admit those paragraphs on that basis. I'm now understanding that that may not be the case, and that Mr. Misetic might be permitted to lead that evidence in a viva voce manner which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear on that matter. If you -- if portions of a 92 ter statement are not admitted into evidence and I can reveal to the parties that your first objection, so I'm not talk about disclosure but about what is opinion and where the element of opinion becomes the prevailing element of the testimony, that that was on the mind of the Chamber. Then, of course, if you call a witness of fact and then to put exactly the same questions would, I take it, result in similar objections. That is, that expert testimony is sought from a witness of fact. At the same time, we do not know how Mr. Misetic will phrase his questions. I mainly wanted to express that he's not prevented from touching upon these subjects, but what was on the back of the mind of the Chamber would certainly result in urging Mr. Misetic to primarily elicit from what the witness knows as far as the facts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does raise some concerns on our part. For example even with respect to the sections of paragraph 7 that the Chamber was inclined to admit, we were disclosed the English article that underlies that paragraph less than 24 hours ago. It's eight pages, single spaces analysis containing literally dozens of figures of various population movements, of various ethnic groups, at various times. We are in no position to assess this information, determine its accuracy. Most of it is totally unsourced. It's based largely on the witness's own analysis as a demographer. And we simply cannot assess it and cannot challenge it, not without, at least, the underlying sources and a significant period of time to assess those sources, consult with our own experts, and produce our only analysis and our own documents in order to challenge the witness's conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which might lead to several procedural approaches. One is Mr. Misetic should not start the examination of the witness; that's -- the other one would be we'd need more time to prepare for cross-examination of the witness. Therefore, we can't proceed to cross-examination immediately after the examination-in-chief has been finished. There are several options in this respect, and it's clear that you have concerns, and I do understand that this is primarily in relation to the demographic courses and consequences of the war against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As well as the analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The journal of social and humanist studies, Pila [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's -- yes, and the analysis referred to in paragraph 7 which is the one I just described to the Chamber. Which is Croatia between immigration and emigration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it your view that examination should not even start in this respect or that you would need more time to consult with experts in order to be able to cross-examine the witness on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to anything in paragraphs 3, 5 and 7, it's our position that examination could not even begin. This is expert analysis. We would need a significant period of time to assess this information and it would be -- it would need to be provided to us with the underlying sources of the witness's analysis which have not been provided and in the form where we can assess the methodology and the manner in which the sources were selected, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond. I strenuously object to the classification of the "Globus" article as an expert opinion. It's not being tendered as an expert opinion. It was published in a magazine in 1998 "Globus." He was the assistant minister. These figures and statistics were part of his job in knowing the demographic statistics. He is not being called in his capacity as a professor at the University of Zagreb, but, rather, in the factual capacity of assistant minister for reconstruction and development. These statistics he was dealing with on a daily basis and, as the witness will testify, were the subject of weekly conversations with members of the international community with whom he participated on a joint working group for refugee returns. So for us to have to provide source information, et cetera, is completely unnecessary and not accurate. It is a factual submission of what he was indicating at the time were the statistics and what he was telling the international community at the time were the statistics, within the scope of his portfolio as an assistant minister. If it will simplify matters, I believe I have indicated that I will not go into paragraph 3 of the statement, and if -- assuming - this is what I indicated to the Prosecution - that there is no dispute that Mr. -- that the witness has knowledge and has a background on these topics and has some basis for -- of knowledge on the area of the demographics in the war. We don't need to get into the specific figures as reported in the report in paragraph 3. So if that will lighten the burden, that's fine. The national programme in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, apparently it does not because this was already discussed on Friday. But I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm saying, Mr. President, we're removing the entire paragraph, so I don't know how that wouldn't alleviate the problem with respect to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Alleviate, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am going through one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That takes care of paragraph 3. Paragraph 5, we are not actually tendering the national programme, and perhaps there was some confusion. This is not -- this national programme was not a scientific study. It was actually a programme approved by the Croatian parliament in 1996 and implemented by this witness in his capacity as assistant minister. If the Prosecution -- other than what's on the page, we're not tendering anything, the underlying document itself, into evidence and so other than -- I mean, for what it is worth, it is mentioned there in paragraph 5, but we're not tendering, nor do we have a copy of the underlying national programme. So I don't want to draw the distinction there between a scientific study and an actual governmental programme that was passed by Parliament. With respect to number 7, again I think I already commented on it. The "Globus" article was published at the time. It has been in his statement as turned over to the -- as uploaded into e-court on the 4th of June -- of this year. It has come to my understanding that the Prosecution was unaware that it was in e-court, and that's what I have been told; however, our position on that has been that we had no notice of the Prosecution had any complaints that all statements hadn't been disclosed that were identified on the 65 ter witness list, so all of this has arisen essentially in the last -- since last Thursday when the Prosecution filed its opposition to the 92 ter statement. And so, in effect, we've had late notice of underlying problems and issues and quite frankly the "Globus" article is because it was turned over to CLSS. Everything else that we had in our control, we turned over on Friday, and, again, just for the sake of consistency, I would recall that it was not not once -- only one time in the Prosecution's case in-chief where we received documents sometimes the night before the witness would come. Mr. Rajcic comes to mind, which was the volume of documents that had no translations for them and we, nevertheless, proceeded and worked our way around it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not the issue that a document was received yesterday. I received numerous documents yesterday. I'm objecting to this eight-page analysis by the witness, which I would like to distribute to the Chamber because the Chamber will see that it's an analysis, demographic analysis, by the witness largely unsourced, with the methodology unclear, and it is impossible for us to challenge the conclusions he draws on paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you offered us something I was about to ask from Mr. Misetic. We would like to spend our break on having a glance on the "Globus" article, and we'll consider whether and what procedural consequences should be attached to the matters you have raised. We'll have a break, and we will resume -- we resume most likely at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on how to proceed, the Chamber would like to know a little bit more about the disclosure issue. Mr. Misetic, you say the "Globus" article was disclosed on the 4th of June; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or uploaded in e-court or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The B/C/S of the "Globus" article, I believe was disclosed on the 4th of May. The translation of the "Globus" article only arrived yesterday from CLSS. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you first: It was disclosed in what context exactly, as in direct relation with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, there's two points on that. The exhibit list was disclosed early last week, and did have that exhibit on it. The statement itself which was -- the witness statement was uploaded into e-court in English on the 4th of June, and I believe the statement makes reference here in paragraph 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's -- it's mentioned as --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The "Globus" article, 1998, April, which is the article that was translated and received from CLSS last night -- or yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber allows the Gotovina Defence to examine the witness in-chief. At the same time, the Gotovina Defence is urged where there is a dispute about whether this witness presents expert opinion or factual information, Mr. Misetic, you're urged through your questions to demonstrate that your position is the right one. Because this is a witness of fact. It's not an expert witness. That means he shouldn't give expert opinion. He also should not give personal opinion. I mean, where it's perhaps a bit more sensitive in this context, because what is personal opinion from someone who apparently has had a demographic career, there we have to be more cautious, as usual, to take care that no personal opinion comes into play.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it wasn't my intention and it isn't my intention to ask him to start drawing conclusions on causes of departure and such issues. I'm mainly interested in, in 1998 what did he say were the numbers of, for example, Serbs that left, Serbs that were coming back, Croats that had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what we then know is what he said without any -- of course, I could have -- I could give a statement at this moment on numbers of Belgians leaving the Netherlands after 1831. I mean, it's worth what it is worth. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's my point, Mr. President, is that I'm not tendering this as: This is a scientific study and, therefore, the Chamber should accept as gospel truth that this is the numbers. What I'm saying is the Croatian government's position in 1998 was this. It can be taken for whatever it is worth by the Chamber, but in looking at the overall context of the issue of refugee returns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Croatian government expressed in 1858 that there were 32 Serbs in a certain village, then that doesn't mean that there were 32 Serbs in a certain village. But it demonstrate what the government at that moment in time said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's fact. Then, of course, the second question is relevance, probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What we're going to go into, Mr. President, is simply to -- in assessing the issue of refugee returns, what was the Croatian' government of the scope of the problem from both the Serb and Croat side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It may that be Ms. Gustafson comes forward and says it is wasn't, hypothetically speaking, 100.000 Croats, it was 50.000 Croats -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, Mr. Misetic, what I would expect Ms. Gustafson to come back with is that is what the position of the Croatian government was, because you're not not presenting these numbers for the accuracy of the numbers, so, therefore, Ms. Gustafson is not -- she doesn't have to respond in that way. Because the thing you're presenting is what the Croatian government, right or wrong, said if, of course, on the basis of other evidence we would finally combining sources that the Croatian government was right or was wrong, of course, then if it is in dispute, then Ms. Gustafson would be wise to challenge the numbers as well. But on the basis of this evidence, but we'll see how it develops, and again, you're urged to put the questions in such a way and the Chamber might even stop the witness if he goes beyond what his factual knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have worked very hard with the witness to try to get him -- I'm just giving advance warning that we're dealing with -- in no disrespect to professors, but he's a professor, I've tried to get him to concentrate on answering my specific question. He understands all my hand signals, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as they are just slow down then it's -- then it's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Stop, slow down, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there are no other signals to be sent to the witness. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I add one thing. Whether or not you should be given more time to prepare for cross-examination is a matter that the Chamber will consider at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just -- I need to express my concerns with what Mr. Misetic just said, because it was based on an assumption that, for example, the number of Serbs who left was fact and not opinion. But the figure that the witness gives in his statement comes from his article, and that figure of 130.000 is clearly based on his analysis in that article of various underlying sources. If those sources are then explored - and I appreciate what Your Honour said about whether something is presented as fact of what the Croatian government represented or not - but if it goes beyond that, then it's our position that this is then -- into the area of witness's expertise in his demographic analyst. That's my concern. My second question really is not -- it's not clear from Your Honours' ruling what the ruling is specifically on the paragraphs of the 92 ter statement which are to be admitted or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have not been tendered yet. We have not heard the attestation of the witness. I can tell you one thing that most likely if it will be tendered, if the attestation is received, that it will be MFI'd and that the main reason for not admitting it would be in paragraphs 3, 5, and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just ask as procedural matter, do you wish for me to go into the factual foundation of paragraph 5 before tendering it or since it is going to be MFI'd anyway should I just do it after tendering it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a rather practical matter, it seems. The Chamber will not decide on whether you do it after or before. Of course, we'll consider, if it is MFI'd, we will consider everything that follows when deciding on admission or not. Then, could we ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sterc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text will now be handed out to you, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sterc. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Good morning to you and everyone else here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Stjepan Sterc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, do you recall meeting with members of the Gotovina Defence on 17 April 2009, 7 May 2009, and 20 May 2009?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall providing a statement to members of the Gotovina Defence on those dates?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement on the 20th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if could I please have on the screen 65 ter 1D2702, please. And with the assistance of Madam Usher, if could I give a hard copy of the statement in Croatian to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, have you had a chance to review that statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that the statement that you signed on the 20th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look on the screen, please, I know you're looking at the hard copy, but if you could also look at the Croatian copy on the screen in front of you, is that your signature in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In reviewing the statement before coming to court, did the statement accurately reflect what you told members of the Gotovina Defence during your interviews?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are there any corrections or clarifications that you believe need to be made to the statement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time you gave the statement to members of the Gotovina Defence, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today that you were asked by member of the Gotovina Defence during your interviews, would you provide the same answers in court today that you provided to members of the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I think so, in view of the complexity of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence or ask that it be MFI'd, pursuant to your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1607, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have explained to the witness the procedure of reading a summary. He is aware of it, and with your leave, I would like to read out a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that include 3, 5 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so but I will certainly try to avoid those three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or would it be better, under those circumstances, to delay the reading of the statement until the end of the testimony? I don't know to what extent the public will still be able to understand the testimony if it has not been read in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
