utterances.text: Mr. President, the only issue that would arise is whether some of the statistics that you said, in terms of the "Globus" article, if that is allowed to be explored, then there's no problem with paragraphs 3 and 5. They're not in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the basis upon which Mr. Misetic represented those figures would be elicited is not the same basis that they appear in the statement, so I'm not sure they could be summarised in a manner that would reflect Mr. Misetic's intention as he just stated to the Chamber in reciting those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'm fully capable of knowing the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's not whether Mr. Misetic understands the distinction. It is whether he can summarise the statement in a way that reflects the manner in which he intends to elicit this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers, exception, the summary to be read at the end of the witness's testimony so as to complete the knowledge of the public rather than to give them already the basis for understanding the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, before we start, I need to remind you again, I am familiar that you have a very high rate of speech, and so I need you to slow down for the purposes of the interpreters and the court reporter in providing your answers, and I will note that I will sometimes try to slow you down because we don't want to miss anything that you're saying. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Sterc, by way of background, what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I'm senior lecturer at the geographical department of the Faculty of Sciences and Mathematics at the University of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just, again, by way of background, you were assistant minister for reconstruction and development from the 11th of October, 1995, until what time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1999. Until the changes in the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After the change of government in Croatia, did you -- what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: After the change in authorities in Croatia, the new government invited me into the government, on to the cabinet, and I was assistant minister for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As assistant minister for reconstruction and development from 11 October 1995 until the change in government, you were directly involved on the issue of refugee returns; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Within the structure of the Croatian government, was there anyone who held a higher position in the Croatian government, in terms of operationally on the issue of implementing programmes of refugee returns?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: On the operative level, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you, as assistant minister, would -- was it fair to say that you would run the day-to-day tasks on the issue of refugee returns?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: That and other affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: To the minister of reconstruction and development.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Mr. Jure Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Within your portfolio, did you have to study demographic statistics and trends?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why demographics, statistics and trends were part of your portfolio?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Because the entire demographic situation in Croatia, especially as linked to the war and after the war, was extremely complex, and a whole series of plans needed to be developed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, develop plans after studying demographics, statistics, and trends?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: After that, since I also led the department for scientific research within the ministry and a huge problem arose with refugees, we had to gear a great part of our efforts to that problem, because we had large problems on a day-to-day basis with the refugees of whom there were, at one point, 750.000 in Croatia. I said 750.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have to study statistics of the ethnic break downs of the occupied parts of Croatia, beginning in 1991 and going through 1995, as part of your portfolio as assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: It was part of my work, because very intensive talks had already started when I arrived at the ministry with the representatives of the international community about this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you explain why the issue of statistics of ethnic breakdowns of the occupied parts of Croatia from 1991 to 1995 were related to your talks with representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Because, together, we wanted to define this whole complex of issues, and before any serious talks started, had to agree about the numbers. The total number of refugees and their structure, the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I would explore some of those numbers. I don't know if you would wish additional foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends on the way in which you will do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. I presumed that the Chamber's ruling still stands and that the exploration of the witness's portfolio -- I'm sorry, I just don't understand where we're going with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that until now it has been established that he studied statistics in that position. If you want to explore them, then it depends in the way in which do you it, Mr. Misetic, whether you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, while you were assistant minister for reconstruction and development, what was your position as assistant minister as to what percentage of Croatia's territory as of 3 January 1992 was outside the control of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: In our estimates, it was around 15.000 square kilometres and around 26.5 per cent of the whole territory of Croatia. However, that's not all. Our estimate was that almost one third of that territory of the Republic of Croatia was out of the control of the authorities, because we also have to take into account the directly -- the area direct next to the front line that was under no one's control, and in the statistics, we recorded it as being under the control of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were assistant minister for reconstruction and development, what was your position as to the ethnic breakdown of the occupied parts of Croatia, according -- in -- in, let's say, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: We made our analyses based on the census of 1991 and estimates were not possible at that time. The results of that analysis were as follows: In the occupied, area at the time of the 1991 census, there were about 50.5 per cent Serbs and 49 -- or, rather, 48.5 per cent of other population, including 37.5 per cent of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's answer has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ambiguous, it seems to me. Mr. Sterc, you said we made our analysis based on the census of 1991 and estimates were not possible at the time. Do I have to understand it as follows: That the numbers you just told us are numbers which are taken from the 1991 census but whether they reflected the actual situation in the territories which were not under your control is uncertain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, these are not the same numbers. We just wanted to show at the beginning of the talks with the international community what the ratios were, based on the 1991 census. In later analyses, we estimated these numbers in specific situations, in specific times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, does this meet your concern?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just concerned as to how we're expected to parse out the -- based on the witness's last answer, what the official position was versus what the analysis was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what happened later, he has given -- he told us that they used different numbers, we do not know about, we have no possibility at this moment to look into the background. One thing that the witness has now answered is that numbers he just gave are based on census figures which do not necessarily reflect the actual situation. Then you could wonder what the probative value of that is, but we'll have to consider that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just -- and I apologise for interrupting, if I could just ask Mr. Misetic to refer to the official position of the Croatian government pursuant to Your Honours' ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Pose the questions [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether he took that position as an assistant minister or whether that was shared by the Croatian government, we could ask the witness always to indicate whether the position he took as an assistant minister, whether that was -- at least to indicate if that position was not shared by the Croatian government as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I would just note that all of these are issues that could be explored in cross-examination, but, you know, getting up and not understanding and those types of objections aren't real objections; but I will do my best to ask him generally if he has any distinction to make between his own position as assistant minister and the overall position of the Croatian government to state that, but I'm not going to ask him after every single question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, not after every single question, but we could ask the witness to indicate whenever any subject is dealt with where he is aware that his position as an assistant minister was not the same as the position of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but my understanding of Your Honour's ruling was that the figures were permitted to be elicited as -- on the basis that they were official positions of the Croatian government, and I would like to insist in regard to that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I think the ruling said it should be factual. Now it could be that some of the numbers were not discussed with the government. What the position of a government or an assistant minister is, is a matter of fact. Whether these are the numbers are accurate is something that could be further explored but it should always be clear whether it is a position taken by a person, which, again, is a factual matter, which requires nothing more than that person or a member of the government saying, This was our position, and then it can be challenged on the basis of documentary evidence; whereas, when we're talking about the accuracy of the numbers themselves, that can be challenged by totally different means. That is, other statistical date, for example. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I may just note, Mr. President, I will again tell him, as you instructed, but I'm asking the question as assistant minister so the question becomes what is the position of -- but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Keep matters very short. Mr. Sterc, a couple of questions have been asked by Mr. Misetic about what your position was as an assistant minister, and I'm talking about the position you held since 1995, not the position you held at a later stage, in a different ministry. Now, if there was ever any dispute about the position you took as an assistant minister with other members of the government, I would like you to always clearly indicate that that was the case. If we do not receive such an indication, the Chamber will understand your answer as being that you, as a member of the Croatian government, and in line with the official position of the Croatian government, took a certain position. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear. Although I feel the need to clarify further. I hope you will give me leave when such situations arise because we are talking about analytical and technical scientific procedures. We, who entered into the talks with the international community, felt the need - and they required it of us - to arrange statistical data and break them down by source and then only proceed with the process of repatriation, return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, what was your position as assistant minister concerning what percentage of the -- let me rephrase it. Of the overall Serb population in Croatia, what percentage lived in unoccupied parts of Croatia and what percentage of that Serb population lived in occupied parts of Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: In the unoccupied part of Croatia, there was a population of a little over 50 per cent of all Serbs in Croatia; and in the occupied areas, .5 or one per cent below 50 of the total population of Serbs in Croatia. So it was almost half/half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would like to explore. Was this a figure you concluded on the basis of the 1991 census, or would it be or before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, as assistant minister, did you take a position as to what happened to the Serb population after 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's calling for an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking for a factual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may finish your question, and the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What happened to the Serb population that lived in unoccupied parts of Croatia after the war started?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: The Serb population that lived in other parts of Croatia, mainly urban areas and the literal area, participated in all the other situations, the economy and the war effort in Croatia together with the rest of the Croatian population. In our estimate, around 70.000 of them left the free part of Croatia and moved to the occupied part of Croatia, or to Serbia, or to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As assistant minister, did you evaluate how many Croats in 1991 lived in occupied parts of Croatia, according to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what position you took?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Out of the total population in the occupied areas of Croatia, according to the 1991 census, there were just over 70 per cent of Croats in the total population of the occupied part of Croatia, which was -- that total was around 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And between 1991 and 1995, what position did you take as assistant minister as to how many Croats were left on that -- on the occupied territory of Croatia before Operation Flash began?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: In our estimate, around five per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, you have, in answer to two questions, told us what your estimates were. The first one was that around 70.000 of the Serbs moved to the parts of Croatia which were not under your control or to Serbia. On what is that estimate based? And, same question, in relation to the estimate -- let me see, the other estimate was about ... one second, please. The five per cent estimate of Croats that remained on the territories which were not under your control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, those were estimates. Those were not official numbers from the census. We had partial sources of information given to us by the international community that we were able to read from Serbian press, and information that we could find in some of their bulletins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Their" is whose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bulletins of the international community, UNHCR, OSCE, and others. They regularly published bulletins and estimated the population there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you combined data from various sources, including newspapers, and that led you to take a certain position. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, your statement, at paragraph 7, discusses an article in "Globus," and before I show that you article, I want it ask you some questions about it. Why did you publish that article in "Globus" in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: In 1998, we had already advanced in our talks with the international community, and the need was felt for the estimated data that we exchanged in our talks to be published somewhere. The estimate was that this should not be published as a -- in the form of a scientific paper because few people read those papers; but, rather, to publish that in -- in something that, in Croatia, was considered an opposition, opposition magazine, which was published in 100.000 copies, roughly. Apart from that, that was also the interest of the editors of that magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your answer you say that the need was felt for the estimates that we exchanged in our talks to be published somewhere. What estimates are you talking about that were exchanged in your talks?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Since we had a grid problem with regard to the alignment of the data, the data that stemmed from our side, the international community, or the Serbian side. So there was the need to give a final estimate with regard to the migrations of population within the former community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification of one of the earlier answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, you explained to us that the estimate was not to be published in the form of a scientific paper, because that would not reach a large public. Now, that is the form on where to publish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you consider the content of the article, the way in which you deal with the data and the conclusions you drew? Did you consider that to be the result of scientific analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that, if not for reaching a larger public, for which reason you published in "Globus," that the content and the character of this article could have been published in a scientific journal as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. [In English] Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have been published as a scientific paper, but writing a scientific paper requires much more time, and since the general -- in the public, at the diplomatic level and at other levels, different data were being put forward very often, and the actual figures were often multiplied. So we felt the need, especially me, because that was within my purview, to publish that to the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But still the result of scientific analysis or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in scientific analyses you cannot quote information from newspapers as relevant scientific evidence, which, of course, does not mean that the information is not correct, but scientific methodology is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you couldn't rely on newspaper articles, although the content, the data, may be correct, which I understand is that you used such sources as newspapers. And what method did you use to verify whether the data in those newspaper articles were or were not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, when such data is published in magazines or bulletins, they are never completely correct. Scientific methodology is such that some deeper-going research is conducted, in order to corroborate that or disprove it. We wanted our final estimates to be put in writing for everyone to be able to read them and comment or give remarks, and then the individual piece of information can either be harmonised or verified anew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have not answered my question. I asked you when you used newspapers as sources, which you said could not be used in, I would say, normal scientific analysis, but apparently you did use, how you were able to verify the accuracy of what was published in those newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't verify. We compared data from the newspapers and the bulletins of the international community, and, based on that comparison, and based on the official data from the census, we were able to estimate what went on in those processes. Apart from that, the Serbs in the occupied areas had something that was called a partial census. Among other things, they often put forward information about their military forces. With regard to the age composition and the gender composition of the average population, and also considering the trends of the natural growth of population, we were able to make such estimates. In some cases, newspaper articles can be verified through official data sources, and they can be enclosed with an authentic scientific paper ; others that cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that the publication and the figures published in this "Globus" article were the result of a -- of the use of various scientifical -- scientific analytical techniques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were possible with regard to the existing data, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I consider this a confirmative answer to my question. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, you, I don't have to explain to you that this sheds some light on what kind of an article this really is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It does. I'm still not sure whether I'm now allowed to show it him or not so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as -- I mean, this Chamber prefers to be transparent in these kind of matters, and it's not our primary purposes -- purpose to stop someone from doing something, but the Chamber expects the parties to show awareness of what the previous testimony was and specifically in relation to this article. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if I could have on the screen 65 ter 1D1559, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, you see on your screen an article. Is that the article in "Globus" which we have been talking about now?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you are the author of the text?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm the author of the text and it -- the text was edited and things were added.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the graphics, are the graphics yours as well?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: The titles on the graphics were added by the editors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court first, in terms of the refugee issue, did Croatia have any refugees from Serbia -- or I should say from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Croatia at the time that you wrote this article?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, based on your recollection, how many refugees from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were in Croatia in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I just ask Mr. Misetic to lay a foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Recollection of what? I don't take it that the witness has counted them personally. So if the witness recollects anything, I would like to know what he recollects, whether that's the statistics used in the government or the outcome of the statistical analysis or scientific analysis of figures. I'd like to know what he's supposed to recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn the page then in the article then since a foundation has been laid for the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had only a short time to go through the article, Mr. Misetic. English page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: English page ... English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sterc, this would be page 3 in the Croatian version. Under the section in the original in the left-hand column, bottom paragraph, written paragraph, and in the English under the section titled "Structure of migration," you wrote: "Up to now, nearly 40.000 Croats left Vojvodina ... about 5.000 Croats left Kosovo and about 4.000 Croats left Serbia and Montenegro making up a total of 49.000. Most of them found accommodation in Croatia." First, can you tell the Court where those numbers came from in your article?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Those numbers were received from the Croatian office for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph says: "By" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could we ask the witness where they got those figures from, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They received the data, based on the registration of those persons in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which included where they came from? I mean, if I register somewhere, would that registration also indicate where that person came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By nationality or by former place of residence? [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By -- there were also data about the birth of the person, the religious affiliations, all data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you used those data to come to conclusions as where they came from or -- because where someone is born is not necessarily the place where he lived before he came to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What that a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was registered, upon new registration in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph says: "By the end of 1992, accommodation was provided in Croatia for nearly 500.000 people from Bosnia and Herzegovina, of whom nearly 400.000 were Croats and a little over 100.000 were Muslims." Can you tell us where you got that information from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: From the same office, the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And along the lines of what the Presiding Judge just asked you, was that the same basis on how you determined where they actually came from as how you determined how many Croats came from Vojvodina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the procedures in place at the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph refers to: "At one point in Croatia accommodation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we finish the present paragraph which reads: "Bosnia-Herzegovina was left with 60 per cent of its 1991 population." What is the basis for that figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the data received from the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, UNHCR reports, and data published in scientific journals, or, indeed, in daily newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you consider, that at the end of 1992 reliable data were available as far as the actual situation in Bosnia was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph says: "At one point in Croatia, accommodation was being provided for about 750.000 people." Where does that figure come from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: The Croatian office for refugees and displaced persons, 750.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the -- in the Croatian to the second column at the top. The next -- skipping that next paragraph and going to the UNHCR initial data and their 1991 and 1992 bulletins: "About 90.000 Serbs left the occupied territory and by the liberation in 1995, their number grew to approximately 140.000." Could you tell the Court, first, where you got the number of 90.000 Serbs; and, second, where you got the number of 140.000 before Operations Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Those were not my estimates. Those were the estimates of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And where did you get these estimates from, from UNHCR? In what form?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Partly from pair bulletins and partly from conversations with them. We talked almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next paragraph says: "During the liberation in 1995, about 130.000 people left the former occupied territory, and it is estimated that around 10.000 people remained after Operations Flash and Storm." First, can you tell the Court where the number of 130.000 people comes from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: When you compare all the data that we spoke about earlier, when you take into consideration the partial census in the occupied area, if you estimate how the military forces, about which they wrote in their bulletins, it was possible to estimate this number of 130.000. In the formerly occupied areas, we supposed that about 10.000 Croats remained there, but we assumed so based on -- on the information that we got after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it 10.000 Croats that you thought?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Ten thousand, 10.000 persons of non-Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So did you ever form an estimate as to how many Serbs had remained in the formerly occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes. But I would have to think now. I think this information can be found in this work. I believe that the number is around 13.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, you earlier give us the number of about 130.000 people that left the -- as you said the former occupied territory. And then you explained when asked where this number comes from, you said: "When you compare all the data that we spoke about earlier, when you take into consideration the partial census in the occupied area, if you estimate the military forces ..." So there are a lot of various sources of information which needed to be interpreted and analysed to come to the figure of 130.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a -- I mean, the conclusion, then, is the number of 130.000 which means that you have -- add numbers, you would add other, perhaps, percentages, you apply an analysis, perhaps a statistic analysis. Do you still have a full list of all the data you used and the methodology you used to reach at this 130.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? We arrive -- I arrived at the number of 130.000 not exclusively relying on these sources, but even earlier, we estimated the number of the Serbs in the free parts of Croatia. We also estimated how many had left the free territory. We also used UNHCR as a -- data to estimate the number of Serb who had left for Bosnia-Herzegovina and other -- and third countries. And adding up all those figures, we estimated the demographic potential in the occupied territories before Operation Storm. That was our procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said that part of the purpose of this exercise was because a lot of numbers were circulating which you didn't agree with. Now, what gave you an opportunity to -- for example, to verify the accuracy of UNHCR numbers, whereas you had doubts as to certain numbers that were circulating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information that was published practically after the operation was about 300.000 persons. This was accepted at the diplomatic level, by journalists, and, generally speaking, publicly, without anyone having -- even tried to apply simple maths, and add up the numbers from various parts of Croatia. And, so to avoid erroneous perception, we wanted to make an official estimate and any scientists, politician, diplomat, journalist was in a position to react to that, but they never did. Why? Because the procedures involved are very complex and whoever analyses a part of Croatia or any other part of the former community must have a very clear picture of the population, the reproduction, the natural growth, emigration, the age of the population. These are demographic parameters which determine the total population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you intend to say that because the demographic parameters were rightly applied in your analysis that, therefore, those who had published wrong figures were not in a position to challenge your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not claiming that. Since I come from science, our procedures are such that, when something is publicly announced, or made public, it can be responded to in writing and in a substantiated way with arguments, so this should be understood as -- an impetus with a scientific approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you earlier asked yourself, Why? I find that on page 69, line 22. You said: "Because the procedures involved are very complex," is it that you wanted to say that they were not on top of these complex issues and, therefore, were not able to respond to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the reason was. I attended many meetings where I was criticised for these estimates in public. In scientific discussions, not in political discussions, that is allowed, but what should follow is a personal analysis producing results and public announcement. Nobody did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Misetic. It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, Mr. Sterc. I already ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to start after the break without the witness, perhaps to briefly discuss how to proceed, in view of the -- where we are on the balance between a witness of fact and an expert testimony. We'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber has considered how to proceed, and the following may be of guidance to you. It became, for the Chamber, apparent, from the testimony of the witness, until now, that the figures in the "Globus" article are mainly the result of scientific analysis of all kinds of sources which are not precisely identified, where we do not know exactly what methods were used to finally reach the figures that are mentioned in there. So, to that extent, this witness, who is a witness of fact, apparently published an article which is primarily the result of scientific analysis, rather than statement of facts. Now, therefore, that doesn't mean that these figures cannot play any role at all, but the facts will then - and I just give an example - will be how were they used. For example let take the figure of 130.000. Was it put forward in any negotiations, was it used as a base of a programme. We don't even have to specify, I would say, about the numbers, can be, for example, a specific number was introduced in negotiations with whomever, then, of course, it may be of importance to further specify. But if, for example, you say, The result of these analysis, we used that as the basis for developing our plans, then we don't have to pay further attention to the figures as such, because the figures reached here, are, as matters stand now in the testimony of the witness, are the result of expert analysis of data available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, two points, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One, I guess I would respectively disagree with that conclusion because there's a mixed issue there, which is the witness is, by profession, an expert or at least he perceives himself to be an expert on the issue; so the question would be could the witness have ever gathered these types of statistics and not approached them in a scientific way given his background. So I'm not sure that that answer has been clarified with the witness. An expert in the field, otherwise dealing with the matter of fact, I would assume, would rely on his own knowledge and expertise in gathering information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind if he relied on it in his work as minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe by way of background he stated that the whole purpose of it was because of negotiations with the international community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then say, Whenever I worked in that field, we used those figures in our negotiations, that's then taken for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe -- if I can look in the transcript, I believe that was in the introduction to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't need -- of course, you could ask him about further details about that, Which figures did you use in preparing a programme, what figures did you use in negotiations with A, B, or C organisation? But the problem is that -- now, let me first give you an opportunity to raise your second point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I guess two more points because one now is brought up by this last issue raised by you, Mr. President. The issue is simply by way of factual background. An issue has been raised by the Prosecution in its case about return of refugees. What we're trying to establish is this person who is the highest ranking person operationally on that question thought how many Serbs had to come back or could theatrically come back to Croatia, how many were coming back as part of his job, how many Croats as of 1998 still had not returned to their homes in the occupied territories which is in the article and which intend to address with him next. That is the purpose of exploring with him what is the actual factual situation on the ground in terms of return of refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what is your perception of the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Their perception, their position, et cetera, because what we're talking about here is the Croatian government's or the assistant minister in charge of the issue his perception of the scope of the problem, the dimensions of the problem; thus far, we have only looked at it in this case through the prism of Serb returnees. What we want to show is that it's a much more complex issue than has been presented thus far, and for that purpose, the numbers as he perceived them are relevant. Whether it turns out it was 170.000 Serbs that had left after Operation Storm or 90.000, is a question that can be debated back and forth. We didn't feel it's an issue for expert testimony because he is not being called here as an independent outside observer to evaluate the -- but rather as a participant who made, then, certain decisions. We are going to get into right now a 100-page plan that was drafted with the statistics in mind, and that plan was implemented on the return of refugees. It is our position you can't understand the plan if you don't understand first the scope of the problem which is multi-faceted. Finally, as a procedural issue, we would just ask that the Chamber keep in mind that we were notified of an issue only on Thursday. These issues had -- had we had more time, and this was such a big problem for the Prosecution, we could have simply postponed this witness for a later date and tried to bring next week's witness in now so that they would have time. So we ask that we not now be penalised because we got late notice that there was issue regarding what this witness was going to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just on the last point, Your Honour. The Defence chose to put forward this witness as a fact witness. They clearly took a chance with that. It is quite clear on the face of the statement that the evidence of the witness is at least on the border-line, and as Your Honours have ruled, fall in parts within the realm of expertise. They took that chance. Now they have an adverse ruling, and there is no question of being unfairly penalised. We responded the same day they tendered the 92 ter exhibit of this witness and I'll repeat I received the underlying material for these paragraphs yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a factual issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any new element to be introduced in this discussion, I would like to hear. Otherwise, I'm quite confident that we could continue it for an hour on the existing controversial, and I'd rather not do that. Anything new, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, I don't consider it to be an adverse ruling; secondly, I don't perceive it to be a game of we're taking chances. What we're trying to do is produce evidence to the Chamber. I think the Prosecution had a certain responsibility to raise issues particularly when a witness list was circulated two or three weeks ago that this witness was coming; third, it is my understanding that Ms. Gustafson was out of the country for two weeks and so some of these issues, it is my understanding, were pushed back until last week when she returned. I have no problem in assisting her with coming back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we then enter into private dealings and whether or not you can be reached when we are abroad, even if I'm on the south pole then I would still deal with matters. Let's -- let's try to keep this a limited debate on the matter. There may be some merit in the positions of both parties in this respect, and the Chamber is more interested in how to proceed fairly to -- or -- Ms. Gustafson, you're not going to tell us where Mr. Misetic went on his last holiday?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I apologise for rising, but I do think there is some confusion because I did understand Your Honours to have made a rule about the -- the evidence of this witness being expert analysis. Mr. Misetic doesn't think there is a ruling. If we could get some clarification from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I said is that the "Globus" article as a basis presents the outcome of scientific analysis which -- where it is difficult at this moment to identify exactly the sources and methodology used, and I urged Mr. Misetic, then, to proceed in how the figures, right or wrong, on what basis, whether invented, copied from "New York Times," "Le Soir," or the local newspaper of The Hague to proceed and see how this material was used as a factual thing for plans, for negotiations, whatever, that's what the Chamber invited Mr. Misetic to do, and I'm sure he will do it. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And with respect to what I was referencing earlier in the transcript in the witness's testimony, this is at page 58, beginning at line 20, and I'll explore it further if the Chamber wishes, but it's where he talks about, We were advanced in our talks with the international community and the need was felt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, that is not -- but I'd like to say -- to hear from the witness, In September we negotiated with this and this organisation, and we used those and those figures, or we did not use these ones, or the others were not relevant, or we waited until after 1995 or -- whatever, but I'd like to make that as factual as possible, because if you say, These figures were used in our discussions, and if then more time is spent on the figures than on the way in which they were used, then I think we are falling back into at least a risk of relying on these data as objectively established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated to you, Mr. President, that was ultimately where I'm getting to once we complete the "Globus" article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's get the witness in so we see how you do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, please be seated. We had a bit of a longer break than we expected, but I hope you'll forgive us. Mr. Misetic will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if we could have page 6 in English on the screen, please, and the last page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the far left-hand column. There we go. Mr. Sterc, in this article in the first paragraph underneath "tragic balance," about the fourth sentence in you write: "And so there are almost 100.000 Croats in Croatia today who were expelled and who are not in their homes in the former occupied areas." Let's stop with that. First of all, where does that figure come from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: That number is from the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons. These are person who is did not return at that time to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why weren't these people in their homes almost three years after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Because, for the most part, their homes had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you discuss with members of the international community the figures concerning how many Croats, as of the publication of this article, still had not managed to be returned to their homes in the occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With whom did you discuss that figure?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: With all the representatives of the UNHCR, OTSS, UTS, the Troika, various diplomatic and other missions in Croatia from the top leaderships to their operative officials, and they claimed that Croatia could not return those 120.000 Croats to the occupied territories for the reasons that I have stated. But that was not perceived as a particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, first let me get the acronyms straight. In line 18 where it says OTSS, can you repeat again what organisation that is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I meant the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then the third acronym, it was interpreted as UTS. Can you recall exactly --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: UNTAES, U-N-T-A-S. The provisional administration in the transitional administration in Podunavlje, in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would you meet with these representatives?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Everyone where. Almost everywhere in Croatia and almost every week we met in the occupied -- Vukovar as guests of the UNTAES. We had negotiations in the occupied Vukovar, in Banja Luka, in Topusko, in Plasko, and most of all in Zagreb, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in those meetings was the figure of 100.000 Croats still not returned to their homes discussed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Because we insisted, in those negotiations, on the principle of everyone returning to their homes, because we thought that was the only right solution for the refugee and displaced persons crisis in Croatia, but most of their actions were, however, focussed on returning the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, you've touched on an issue that I intended to get to later, but it may be relevant here so maybe you can explain it. You talk about the principle of everyone returning to their homes, and then you also talk about "... most of their actions, were, however focussed on returning the Serbs." And I'd ask to you please explain to the Chamber what is, or what was the principle of everyone returning to their homes, and how was it related to the issue of Serbs returning to their homes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Well, that is a fundamental principle in resolving the crisis of refugees and displaced persons. That's one. Second, since homes were occupied in Croatia and in Podunavlje and in Bosnia-Herzegovina by all sorts of people, we had start moving the whole complex of these issues by raising it to the highest level and that required financial, logistical, and organisational support, because that would help resolve the entire complex situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Was the issue of the return of Croats to their homes relate to the issue of the return of Serbs to their homes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber why these issues are related.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Because everything was so interwoven and that refugees came to Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia from all over the place, and the numbers were so large and the directions of their movement could not be controlled by anyone. They took the line of least resistance, and they just occupied whatever buildings were vacant or were on their way and happened to be intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As part of this issue of the interwoven-ness of the problem, did you gather -- did you conduct statistical analyses to determine the extent of the problem?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: We made weekly estimates at meetings of the Working Group, with representatives of the international community. Our numbers did not always match, but we tried in all our actions and discusses to harmonise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say "weekly estimates." Weekly estimates of what types of statistics?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Those were estimates primarily from the UNHCR, Croatia, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But what were you estimating?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: We estimated the number of persons in Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, respectively; where they had come from and where they should return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to the "Globus" article, these statistics, were they discussed at these weekly meetings of the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we continue on, we talked about the 100.000 Croats in Croatia. The next sentence says: "About 120.000 Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina are all over Croatia in various kinds of accommodation; 80.000 Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina in Germany are waiting to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina ... 40.000 Croats from Vojvodina have been provided accommodation in various ways in the Republic of Croatia and ... 5.000 Croats from Kosovo were also provided accommodate addition in various ways in the Republic of Croatia. "And so in all, about 395.000 Croats are not in their homes." So the statistics that I have read right now, were any of these statistics discussed at the meetings of the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which of these statistics were discussed at the meetings of the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I can give you an example. Say, the Croats from Kosovo, our estimate was, and that of the Office of Refugees and Displaced Persons, that they were about 5.000. In accordance with the policy of everyone returning to their homes, I also asked for these people to return -- or, rather, put forward a proposal for these people to return to their homes at the meeting of the joint Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Moreover, we wanted Croats -- the Croats to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina to their homes from Croatia; of course, under the assumption that they wanted to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But of the statistics that we have read out, in other words, how many Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina were in Croatia, how many Croats were from Bosnia were in Germany, how many Croats from Vojvodina were in Croatia, were those statistics discussed at meetings of the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. But the positions were along the following lines. That is a matter for Croatia to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was your position when you would be told that this was a matter for Croatia to deal with?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: My position was that, among others, it is the interest of Croatia that Croats, among others, should return to their homes in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, and that the international community should take part in that, as we're speaking about the return to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there any relationship between you raising these issues of Croats returning to their homes and the international community's insistence on Serbs returning to their homes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Both were illogical. All of us doing that job were to accept that general principle and work to enable both groups to return to their homes. Because that was the basic principle, repatriation, return to their homes. We knew, of course, that some of those people for various reasons didn't want to return, but we should enable everybody who is willing to return to indeed return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we spoke about statistics before the war period, how many of various ethnic groups were where in 1991 and how many members of which ethnic groups were where in 1995. Were those statistics discussed at meetings of the joint Working Group and why, if so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Of course, they were discussed. All of these articles I published were used by the international community, once they had them translated, and at our meetings which tried to harmonise them because sometimes they would express their doubts about some data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This article in "Globus," you mention: "Articles I published were used by the international community." Was this article in "Globus" used by the international community, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know so? Do you have any knowledge that they did?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure; I can only suppose. Because we spoke about those figures, so it's logical to assume that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was your motivation, what was your purpose in publishing this work in "Globus"? And was it related to your work on -- if at all, on the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a link. It was our wish to have that published to -- to launch discussion about that, and, if necessary, have data corrected; and, finally, agree on the number of people to be returned to their homes, in accordance with the principle of everybody returning to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is even more specific, which is: Why was it your wish to have it published; and why was it important to you to launch a discussion about the number of people to be returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: You mean me personally as the chairman of the joint Working Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let's start with you personally. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: It mattered to me personally because we were unable to harmonise figures in many -- on many occasions. Because many things have to be harmonised, such as finances, and the entire logistics, and the great pressures that we have spoken about often should be reduced to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your answer is: "We were unable to harmonise the figures." Who is we?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I mean primarily the representatives of the international community who, at the outset, were saying that 300 [as interpreted] persons left Croatia during and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 300 persons or 300.000 persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Persons? Or just in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Persons, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, among those persons the Serbs were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did this article, this publication in "Globus," have any effect on harmonising the figures of persons that needed to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC
utterances.text: It certainly did. Because we had a basis for discussion and harmonisation. I can also add that there were also -- there was also criticism to what I published, because some people claimed that what I had published was unfounded. There was even a discussion about that at public meetings or conferences, one such instance being the conference the Serbs in Croatia organised by the Croatian Helsinki Committee, where I also took part and discussed, et cetera, but never did anyone put forward other data in an analytical fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification of one of the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I can just tell you, Mr. President, I don't have any other foundational questions to put to him, so if the Chamber does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to invite you, if you have other questions on foundation, I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that the publication in "Globus" had certainly an effect on harmonising the figures of persons that needed to return because, as you said, "... we had a basis for discussion and harmonisation." Was ever any agreement reached on what would be the basis on which to further proceed in the -- with the international organisations? I mean, did you finally say, Okay, let's work on the basis of this and this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, eventually, we were able to harmonise that, and the final figures resulted in the programme of return and providing care for all persons. That programme was adopted by the Croatian government and this is an outcome of all these -- this process of harmonisation and negotiations and that programme has been in use until this day, with minor changes. And I believe that it is also used in other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that accepted then by the Working Group? I'm trying to understand what harmonising exactly means. That apparently there was a dispute [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Primarily in the Working Group. All these talks and negotiations in the Working Groups was not confrontation. Nobody accused anyone, nobody tried to force anyone to do anything or insist on anything. We were simply trying to find a solution and to get the -- this complex process going in various directions and come up with one document that would be applicable. And this whole story that had to do with displaced persons and refugees should be transferred from the political to the humanitarian level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is still not an answer to my question. Apparently there was disagreement about the figures between the Croatian government, I take it, and the international organisations which would be involved in -- in return issues. You said this article being published certainly had an effect on harmonising. Then I asked you, What was the result of that? Was finally -- was there agreement on the -- in the joint Working Group on these matters? And then you said, Well, finally, we -- we had this programme, which seems to be a Croatian government programme. While I did understand that there was no problem within the Croatian government, but it was the Croatian government and the international organisations and institutions. What I'm asking, quite simply, is: Was there ever any agreement where the international organisations and institutions agreed with the Republic of Croatia on, this is the number of people that migrated in this direction; we accept that as the basis for plans, and if so - because I'd like to know what then the agreement was - was there such an agreement, and, if so, is there any documentation about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the figures were harmonised. And after that harmonisation in the Working Group what followed were the other documents. And not only them, but also our public talks on Croatian television about all the issues that we're discussing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I would expect if there is a harmonisation of the figures, if there's any agreement on that, that at least it would have been written down somewhere because you might easily forget about that numbers. Is there any document in which it said, Well, we discussed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is the very programme that I mention where the figures or numbers are explicitly mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that was a Croatian programme. Is it anywhere apparent in that document that this was not just the Croatian view but also accepted, meanwhile, by other institutions or organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. The negotiations about the adoption of the programme we're talking about, I conducted personally with Tim Guldimann, the chief of the OSCE mission to Croatia, and with Mr. Robertson, the representative of UNTAES, and other organisations. And we agreed on all that in the Working Group, about the basics. Of course, the programme is much more complex. We're speaking about a 100-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I leave it further in the hands of Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic, yes, I know that we're close to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I indicated, Mr. President, I don't have any additional foundational questions to ask, unless you wish me to ask something else. But at this point, I would ask that the "Globus" article be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be MFI'd. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will have a further opportunity to argue whether it should be admitted, yes or no. We will do that at a later stage. Mr. Misetic, we'll adjourn for the day. But you understand that it might be a difficult question to answer, how much time would you need for the examination-in-chief, because I'm well aware that the Chamber may have confused what you on your mind at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You never confuse me, Mr. President. It just took a little longer than I anticipated, but I would hope to finish in the first session tomorrow. Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I am aware that I'm putting a similar difficult question to you. Could you give us any indication as to how much time would you need, assuming that you could start, which is not yet determined.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I certainly start on certain parts of the statement. That's not a problem. And for the rest of it, it depends what happens. At this point, I anticipate three to four hours on the basis of the paragraphs of the statement that are not contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I inappropriately had not asked the Cermak and Markac Defence on whether and how much time -- whether they have any questions and how much time they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment there are no questions arising, and I will keep that position under review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point, no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sterc, we adjourn for the day, and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony whether already given or still to be given. I already invite Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom because we have to assign a MFI number to the "Globus" article. And we would like to see you back, just for your information, Mr. Sterc, we will have our hearing tomorrow in the morning. We start at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D1559 will become Exhibit D1608, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status for the time being. We'll adjourn and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, 15th of July, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
